newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia minority party says it has enough seats.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia minority party says it has enough seats.

text.p: The minority Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) said on Saturday it had enough seats in the national parliament to function, despite a drastic fall in its share of the vote in last month's general election.

The secretary-general of the government-recognised faction of the PDI, Buttu Hutapea, said in a statement received on Saturday that the party would have the legal minimum 11 seats in the national parliament, down from 56 seats in the last parliament.

"Considering the votes received and the steps taken by the PDI thoroughout Indonesia, it can be confirmed that the PDI has recieved 11 seats in the next national parliament," Hutapea said in the statement.
The ruling Golkar party won a record 74 percent of the vote in an election campaign marred by violence and a poll tainted by widespread allegations of manipulations and irregularities.

A PDI official at party headquarters said on Saturday the party would have two seats each from the provinces of North Sumatra, Central Java and East Java as well as one from West Java, West Kalimantan, Irian Jaya, East Nusa Tenggara and East Timor.
"What is clear is that the PDI has never begged or asked for pity from anybody," Hutapea said in the statement.

Provisional results of the poll had shown the Golkar party won 325 seats in the House, the United Development Party (PPP) 89 and the PDI 10, after the counting of 115 million ballots. The final results will be announced on June 23.

The drastic drop in the PDI's vote followed a split in the volatile Christian-Nationalist alliance last year which led to ousted leader Megawati Sukarnoputri urging supporters to boycott its campaign and not vote for the government-recognised faction.
Megawati and her supporters were not officially recognised and not allowed to run in the tightly controlled poll.

Under current rules, each of the three parties contesting the election must have at least one representative assigned to each of the 11 commissions that carry out the bulk of work in the 500-seat assembly.

The government had lobbied the PPP, which won 23 percent of the votes in the May 29 poll, to grant some of its votes to the PDI, which secured only three percent, down from 15 percent in the last poll in 1992.
But the Moslem-backed party said it would play by existing electoral laws and would not transfer some of its votes to the PDI after it appeared its rival would not gain the required minimum.
The idea of vote transfers came from the Golkar party, which exceeded its official target of 70.02 percent of the vote and said it was willing to grant some of its votes to the PDI.

The Jakarta Post on Saturday quoted the deputy secretary of the government's election committee, Walujo, as saying on Friday it had given up its efforts to increase the PDI's vote after the three recognised parties could not come to a consensus.
Besides the 425 legislators elected last month, the parliament has 75 appointed members of the armed forces who do not vote.
